EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
This report provides a summary of the investigation of prototype infrared diode laser-based sensors
intended to continuously monitor carbon dioxide (CO2). Their principal purpose is to discern anomalous
temporal or spatial changes resulting from local CO2 emissions that may indicate leakage from carbon
capture and storage (CCS) reservoir sites or related pipeline and wellhead infrastructure.  The initial
applications are intended to be for personnel safety and pipeline leak inspection. The sensors also have
potential beneficial uses for environmental monitoring. The prototype equipment was designed by
Physical Sciences, Inc., and was field tested in Champaign, Illinois and Decatur, Illinois as part of the
Illinois Basin – Decatur Project (IBDP) being led by the Illinois State Geological Survey (ISGS). Three
sensor configurations based on infrared tunable diode laser absorption spectroscopy (TDLAS) were
investigated: (i) an Open-Path Sensor (OPS) for CO2 which measures path-integrated carbon dioxide
concentrations over a fixed path to monitor along pipelines and at wellheads, (ii) a Remote Carbon-
Dioxide Leak Detector (RCLD) which is a compact and mobile diagnostic tool intended for pipeline
surveying, and (iii) an In-ground Sensor (IGS) intended for monitoring carbon dioxide levels in shallow
wells or subsurface agricultural drainage systems. Two of these sensors, the OPS and RCLD were
deployed and tested at the Illinois Basin - Decatur Project (IBDP) site in Decatur, Illinois.  Efforts
towards constructing and deploying the IGS were made, including delivery of several components, layout
of power and data collection support equipment, and plans for field deployment. However, a specialized
infrared laser component was not functional and a suitable replacement could not be obtained before the
project ended. Therefore, the construction of the IGS configuration could not be completed. This report
includes a summary of project goals, TDLAS theory, components of each CO2 sensor system, and key
results obtained in laboratory and field testing.  The challenges associated with each diagnostic are
discussed, and lessons learned are summarized. The collaborative investigations of Physical Sciences Inc.
and the Illinois State Geological Survey for this program have illustrated the uses of TDLAS-based
sensors. More specifically, two types of CO2 sensor and monitor configurations were tested successfully
at the IBDP site. Both demonstrated detection and identification of abnormal CO2 releases from wellhead
pipelines. With refinements, similar systems could be used at other CCS sites as part of an integrated leak
detection and environmental monitoring strategy.

I.    PROJECT INTRODUCTION
The report is a summary of a U.S. Department of Energy (DoE) funded Small Business Technology
Transfer (STTR) Phase II project extension in which the Illinois State Geological Survey (ISGS) served
as a subcontractor to Physical Sciences Inc. (PSI). The performance period of the project extension was
June 16, 2012 through November 14, 2013. The goal of the ISGS investigation was to demonstrate
prototype infrared diode laser-based sensors at an active CCS project in Decatur, Illinois, USA. These
types of sensors have promising potential to be used for CO2 leakage detection as part of environmental
monitoring programs at carbon sequestration sites.

A. Overview of the Illinois Basin Decatur Project
The Midwest  Geological  Sequestration  Consortium (MGSC,  see  www.sequestration.org  [1])  is
conducting a demonstration-scale CCS project in Decatur, Illinois, USA to test the ability of a deep saline
formation to store one million tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO2) from an ethanol production facility. In
November 2011, CO2 injection began at a rate of 1,000 tonnes per day and will continue for three years
into the Mount Simon Sandstone, a deep saline reservoir, at a depth of approximately 2,100 meters (7,000
feet).

An extensive Monitoring, Verification, and Accounting (MVA) program has been undertaken for the
Illinois Basin – Decatur Project (IBDP) and is focused on the 0.65 km2 (0.25 mi2) project site.  Near-
surface and subsurface monitoring are integral efforts to reach MVA and project goals of 1) establishing
pre-injection conditions to evaluate potential impacts from CO2 injection, 2) demonstrating that project
activities are protective of human health and the environment, and 3) quantifying and tracking CO2 stored
in the Mount Simon Sandstone reservoir. The IBDP MVA Program is a combined effort of the ISGS,
Archer Daniels Midland (ADM) Company, Schlumberger Carbon Services (SCS), Schlumberger Water
Services, PSI, Lawrence Berkley National Laboratory, University of Illinois, TRE-Canada and the Carbon
Capture Project, and the Illinois Department of Transportation.  More than 20 different monitoring
methodologies are being used at IBDP to field test the efficacy of those methods to monitor large-scale
CCS projects.

Near-surface  monitoring  efforts  include  near-infrared  color  aerial  imagery  acquisition,  surface
deformation monitoring, net CO2 flux monitoring, soil CO2 flux monitoring, soil gas sampling, high-
resolution electrical earth resistivity surveys, and shallow groundwater sampling. Subsurface monitoring
efforts include 2D seismic surveying; 3D seismic and vertical seismic surveying; passive seismic
monitoring; injection zone temperature, pressure, and fluid monitoring; above caprock temperature,
pressure, and fluid monitoring; and open and cased hole logging. Environmental monitoring was initiated
in 2009 and is currently scheduled to conclude in 2017 after the three-year injection and three-year post-
injection periods have concluded. On-going injection operations are being conducted under a Class I –
non-hazardous underground  injection  control (UIC)  permit  issued by  the  Illinois Environmental
Protection Agency. A Class VI UIC permit application was submitted to the U.S. Environmental
Protection Agency in December 2011 for the IBDP and is currently under review.

C. TDLAS Prototype Device Configurations
For this project, PSI focused on building and testing three prototype sensor configurations for leak
detection using tunable diode laser absorption spectroscopy (TDLAS).  The sensor configurations
included:

  1. An “open-path” sensor (OPS)  that continuously monitors CO2  levels along a  line of  sight
      approximately 100 m long, intended as an alarm-type system for personnel safety that would be
     used along pipelines and at wellheads;
  2. An “in-ground” CO2 point sensor (IGS) intended to provide long-term continuous measurement of
    CO2 concentrations and changes over time from a shallow subsurface installation (e.g., agricultural
      drain, groundwater monitoring well); and
  3. A remote carbon dioxide leak detector (RCLD) that is a hand-held, portable device intended for
    CO2 pipeline leak surveying and detection.

The sensors were intended to 1) provide CO2 monitoring data from field equipment with limited
maintenance needs and 2) be operated by end users with minimal need for advanced operational training.
The IBDP site was an excellent location for field testing, because  it had an extensive environmental
monitoring program already in place that would complement sensor testing.


II.   TDLAS CONCEPT AND THEORY
The three sensor systems discussed here all apply TDLAS using infrared semiconductor lasers and
photodetectors to measure the infrared absorption of CO2. The method takes advantage of the fact that
CO2 molecules absorb infrared (IR) radiation on well-known, narrow-wavelength bands centered on
specific wavelengths in the infrared electromagnetic spectrum. The PSI sensors operate in the near-IR at
wavelengths in the 1.5 µm and 2.0 µm spectral regions.

Figure 1 shows the basic layout of a TDLAS sensor. The simple layout consists of 1) a tunable infrared
laser which is tuned in its center wavelength and intensity by modulation of the current; 2) an optical path
which traverses a region bearing the IR absorbing gas of  interest  (in  this case CO2); and 3) a
photodetector. Figure 2 illustrates the basic signal relationships used in determining absorption along the
optical path of the laser. The laser current is modulated at a frequency (fm) resulting in a modulation of

                                          3

intensity at the detector, creating a component of the detector signal at frequency  fm.  This signal
component is called F1. As the laser current modulates, the laser wavelength also modulates over the line
shape of a CO2 absorption feature.  During a single current modulation sweep, the laser wavelength
passes through the shape of the absorption feature twice, resulting in a component of the detector signal
amplitude modulation  at 2*fm.   This signal component  is called  F2.  The OPS signal processor
demodulates the periodic signal to measure the RMS amplitudes of F1 and F2, and these components are
used to calculate the CO2 concentration. F1 is a measure of the laser power received at the detector; it is
generally free of influences from other sources of optical power, such as sunlight, that impinge of the
detector. F2 is proportional to the product of received laser power and path-integrated CO2 concentration.
Thus, the ratio F2/F1 provides a measurement that is directly proportional to CO2 and is independent of
received laser power.  This feature enables the sensors to correctly track CO2 despite changes in laser
power transmitted across the optical path. As seen in some of the data illustrations below, such changes
occur due to variability in reflectance of illuminated backscatter surfaces, precipitation in the optical path,
thermally-induced  movements  of  optical  components  affecting  alignment,  and  the  like.  The
proportionality constant that converts the measured F2/F1 to CO2 concentration is generally determined by
calibrating the sensor with a known amount of CO2 in the laser path.

III.   OPEN-PATH SENSOR
This section is a summary of the deployment experiences of the OPS at the IBDP site in Decatur, IL. The
OPS uses  near-infrared TDLAS  to measure CO2 absorption over a 100 m  path-length,  situated
immediately north of the injection well/pipeline, with the path running east (laser transceiver) to west
(reflector). Thus, the laser passes over the 100-m path twice, being launched from the transceiver toward
the reflector, and then returning along the same path to the transceiver collection optics.  The OPS
transceiver continuously transmits CO2 absorption data via radio to the data-logging workstation setup in
the trailer to the south of the injection well.

The OPS was initially deployed at the IBDP site on January 7, 2013 and is planned to be retrieved in
December 2013. An aerial view of the deployment location is shown in Figure 3. Because only relative
CO2 values need be measured to perform the intended leak detection function, the sensor was not fully
calibrated upon deployment; the installed calibration constant was an approximately value based on prior
testing at the PSI facility. As discussed below, near the completion of the test period data were acquired
with an alternate CO2 sensor, thus enabling OPS calibration to yield absolute CO2 values.





 Figure 3. Location of PSI TDLAS beam line for field testing of prototype CO2 Open-Path Sensor (OPS)

A. OPS Operation and Components
The PSI OPS takes advantage of the near-infrared absorption spectra of the CO2 molecule in order to
determine CO2 levels along its optical path. The device has four primary components:

    A fiber coupled tunable infrared diode laser,
     Primary optics which launch the fiber-coupled laser beam along the absorption path,




                                          5

  A passive directionally-reflective target (fabricated from a commercial Stop sign partially covered
     with reflective tape) at the opposite end of the absorption path which returns laser radiation back to
      the transceiver, and
    Secondary optics which collect the returned laser radiation on to an infrared sensor.

Additional components to the system include (i) a lithium ion battery which is periodically recharged by a
solar panel and supplies power to the transceiver components, (ii) a wavelength modulation spectroscopy
circuit board which controls the tunable laser, and analyzes the sensor data, (iii) a wireless radio modem
which transmits the board data to a workstation, and (iv) a workstation which collects the transmitted
circuit board data, performs calculations, and logs data for later use and inspection.

C. Challenges of Deployment
During OPS testing, a few challenges were encountered and are summarized below.

   Power Supply Issues (Budgeting)
Despite PSI reporting nearly one-year of solar-powered operation during testing of the OPS in Andover
MA, when installed at the IBDP site the unit initially experienced intervals of insufficient charge causing
loss of data.    Given the known transceiver system  (laser, transceiver board, radio,  etc.) design
specifications, the sensor power requirements are well-defined, but variable weather conditions made it
difficult to specifically predict the power available for the solar panel-based recharging system. Shadows
from adjacent infrastructure also reduced sunlight availability for system charging.

During spring 2013, the 19 amp-hour (AH) battery (Southwest Electronic Energy Group #7719069 Four
Series {SWE www.swe.com}) used in the OPS was not well sustained by the 30-W solar panel installed
initially. Using recommended equipment from PSI, the voltage and current data of the power supply
system were analyzed. LASCAR USB voltage data loggers (EL-USB-3) were used to monitor the
voltage at the panel input and the battery output terminals. A Sperry DM-6450 digital multimeter was
used as an ammeter to measure the current between the solar panel and the OPS battery, and the current
from the battery to the laser/sensor board and radio (at varied data logging rates).  Table 2 shows
representative data of system voltages and currents for various cloud cover conditions, along with
comparison of the panel power to the power used by the OPS (assuming a 12-hour charging period). The
data indicated that the panel power was not sufficient to sustain OPS through extended periods of heavy
cloud cover. To resolve this condition, the 30W solar panel was replaced by a 65-W panel on 10/18/13.

   Thermo-mechanical Alignment Drift
TDLAS applications require well-designed optics.  Factors that must be considered are path length, the
beam divergence and far-field shape, the collection optics field-of-view, reflector sizing, and the rigidity
of the mechanical components.  Various structural components flex due to heating, which leads to
changes in alignments of the optical components. During installation, components (specifically aiming of
the laser at the reflective target) are aligned to optimize the received laser power.  Any subsequent
changes in alignment cause received laser power to diminish from the optimum. As described previously,
in general the CO2 measurement is unaffected by these changes. However, there is a minimum amount of
laser power that must be received to preclude noise and errors in the CO2 measurement.  The sensor
automatically recognizes when the received power is too small for proper measurement.  In its current
configuration, when the F1 signal is too small an error code is written in the data file, but CO2 data is still
reported, albeit possibly erroneously.

The current version of the OPS prototype uses a modified commercial telescope with the fiber collimation
optics and a launch reflector mounted at the front of the telescope and a sensor mounted in place of the


                                          7

telescope objective. While this configuration served well for demonstration purposes, a design similar to
that applied in the RCLD would be more robust and is recommended. With this modification the OPS
could serve  as a more  robust alarm  sensor, and  potentially  also as a  calibrated  diagnostic  for
environmental monitoring applications.

   Environmental Factors and Scheduling
A few environmental factors were observed during the OPS deployment and should be considered in
future OPS deployments including:

     Interruption of data due to vehicles, people, animals, etc. blocking the IR beam path.  If possible,
      signs should be posted to identify the path and limit beam interruption.  Elevating the laser path
     above traffic may help limit these interruptions.
     Structures on-site should be taken into consideration when positioning the solar panels such that
     good sun exposure is guaranteed throughout the year, and a schedule for repositioning the panel as
      necessary should be made.  At the IBDP deployment location, an overhead pipeline periodically
      cast a shadow on the OPS solar panel reducing available sunlight for proper system charging.  In
      appropriate locales, solar power may be supplemented or replaced by wind power.
     Firmness of the reflector/target installation: there were some issues with wind knocking down the
      metal-sign reflector used for the OPS. This could be remedied using a more permanent (concrete)
      or more stable (larger base) installation.
    Radio data-logging: The radio power level and antenna system should be set up such that clear,
      uninterrupted communications are established between the OPS transceiver and the data logging
      workstation.
     Clear communications were needed with facilities managers and pipeline operators to identify
      variations in absorption that were due to normal operation (as opposed to actual unintended
       releases). At the IBDP site, no unintended releases occurred, but several routine releases (i.e., CO2
      pipeline blowdowns prior to startup of injection operations) occurred and were used as signals of
      opportunity to test the OPS responses.    In addition, frequent communications with facilities
      personnel were important to adequately understand and document interruptions in OPS signals that
     were related to physical blockages (i.e., parked vehicles) that interrupted the sensor beam.

    Initial Testing
Some initial tests were performed after deployment to verify that the OPS would respond to CO2
in its path using an infrared transparent bag filled with CO2 at the reflector surface and multiple

E. OPS Performance Observations
Given below is a summary of significant observations and lessons learned.

    As expected, the OPS concentration measurement (ppm-m) scaled linearly with distance while F1
      decreased as d-2.
    The OPS responded promptly to changes in CO2 during routine pipeline blowdown, illustrating its
       utility as a permanent monitor to detect and report unintended leakage.
    The OPS was not calibrated to report absolute CO2 concentrations. CO2 values calculated by the
      real-time software were typically a factor of 2 smaller than comparison measurements acquired
     with LI-COR instruments.
     Installation of the wireless solar-powered transceiver was straightforward and simple.
    The procedure for aiming the OPS laser beam at the reflective target, aided with a 50 milliwatt 650
    nm fiber-coupled “fault-locator” attached to the launch fiber in place of the IR  laser, was
      straightforward over the 100-m path.
    The 30-W solar panel was insufficient for sustaining power to the OPS in poor weather conditions
     and was replaced with a 65-W panel (10/18/13).
    The 19.3 Ah Li-ion battery selected for the OPS performed well throughout the evaluation at IBDP,
      despite numerous charging and discharging events due to lack of charging current in poor weather
      conditions.
    Low return signal, believed due to thermo-mechanically induced alignment degradation of optical
     components, occasionally resulted in loss of data.  Launch and collection optics designed for
     reduced thermal sensitivity would enhance system autonomy. (PSI notes that this modification has
     been made to an OPS methane sensor being demonstrated elsewhere, and indeed demonstrates
      significantly less alignment drift over ~200m laser pathlengths.1)

B.  Analysis of Transistor Outline-style Laser Failure Issues
All of the components required to assemble the sensor head with the exception of the infrared diode laser
component were delivered to the ISGS.  Subsequently, one of two VCSELs used in the design was
delivered to the ISGS by PSI.  However, the VCSEL was nonfunctional when delivered to the ISGS,
having failed in the PSI laboratory just prior to sensor shipment after several months of operation. The
second VCSEL had previously failed in similar fashion. PSI contacted the VCSEL supplier concerning

The failure analysis indicates a potential incompatibility among this particular VCSEL product, the sensor
configuration, and PSI laser control electronics. Circuitry modifications to further suppress susceptibility
to ESD are likely to resolve the problem.  Without such modifications, confidence in a successful in-
ground sensor deployment that will yield long-term data is low.  Unfortunately, replacement VCSELs
require 3-6 months for delivery, and must be followed by several months of laboratory testing to verify
that the sensor modifications were successful.  Therefore, final construction of the IGS could not be
completed during the project period and the instrument was not deployed at the IBDP site.


V.   REMOTE CARBON-DIOXIDE LEAK DETECTOR
This section summarizes the modification of a Heath Consultants Remote Methane Leak Detector
(RMLD) to measure carbon dioxide absorption, and the laboratory and field testing of the modified
device.

A. Modification of the RMLD to Measure CO2 Concentration
During March 19 to 22, 2013, ISGS staff (J. Zimmerman) traveled to PSI in Andover, MA to work with
PSI staff (M. Frish, M. Laderer, and R. Wainner) on modification of a Heath RMLD ([6]) for detection of
CO2, to develop a fabrication and testing plan for the prototype IGS, and to receive training on operation
and maintenance of both devices.

Modification of the RMLD for CO2 detection involved: a) substituting the RMLD’s methane-specific
10mW 1.6μm DFB laser with a CO2-specific 3mW 2.0µm DFB laser in a drop-in replacement fiber-
coupled 14-pin butterfly package; and b) replacing the RMLD’s InGaAs detector and pre-amp with an
extended InGaAs detector and matched pre-amp sensitive to 2.0 µm light. This combination of laser and
detector installed in the RMLD transceiver was expected to provide a useable standoff range of about
10m when aimed at a diffuse (i.e., non-reflective) scattering surface, as compared to the standard RMLD
which typically provides standoff detection range up to 30m.





                 (a) IR Laser Control Module                               (b) Transceiver
  Figure 13. Interiors of Modified RMLD components: (a) IR laser control module, and (b) transceiver.

Using PSI control board software, the modified detector (shown in Figure 13, hereafter referred to as the
Remote CO2 Leak Detector, RCLD), was tuned in laser operating temperature and current by monitoring
the absorption of ambient CO2. The laser was set to operate at 90 mA and 22.9 °C, which corresponds to
an operating wavelength of 2.004 µm (or 4990 cm-1 in wavenumbers), overlapping a CO2 absorption
feature.  This operating condition was selected in order to avoid the strong H2O absorption features at
4989 and 4993 cm-1. The modulation current depth was set at 17 mA corresponding to a wavelength
sweep range of approximately 0.2 nm (or 0.5 cm-1).  Like the OPS, the RCLD was not calibrated to
provide absolute measurement of CO2, but comparison with LI-COR instrument measurements described
below provides the information needed to complete such a calibration. They show that the reported ppm-
m values should be multiplied by (1/0.55 = 1.82).

D. RCLD Field Testing
An initial deployment of the RCLD was made on May 6, 2013 to test operation, and handling in the field,
with additional deployments at IBDP in July to measure CO2 from a pipeline blowdown procedure during
injection startup operations, and in October to make comparisons with the OPS and LI-COR LI-8100A.

   Measurements vs. Distance with Various Reflectors
The RCLD was field tested at the IBDP injection well site, collecting CO2 measurements as a function of
distance from various target surfaces.  These surfaces include corrugated metal trailer exterior walls,
container and vehicle doors, concrete barriers, and the reflective Stop sign used as the OPS target.
Examples of these data are shown in Figure 16. The reflective stop sign (OPS target) provided a strong
return signal (F1, not plotted) from ranges exceeding 20m, yielding a path-integrated CO2 measurement
that is linearly proportional to standoff distance.  The other diffuse scattering surfaces, as expected,
suffered relatively weak return signals at standoff distances exceeding about 5m. With these weak but
detectable signals, the RCLD is programmed to reduce noise at the expense of calibration accuracy while
maintaining  ability to detect leaks as indicated by changes in  relative, rather than absolute, CO2
concentration. Thus, at ranges >5m, the RCLD response does not increase linearly with standoff distance.
Return signals are too weak to elicit response at ranges beyond 10-15m depending on the diffuse target
surface. This is consistent with design expectations.

VI.   STATUS OF SENSORS

A. OPS
On November 8, the OPS was operational at the IBDP site. The current plan is to conduct a fully
autonomous test of the system beginning November 15, and to retrieve the device from the field on
December 16. Further deployment plans for the OPS are being discussed.

B. IGS
The majority of components for the IGS sensor head are currently at the ISGS in Champaign, Illinois.
The malfunctioning laser components were returned by PSI to the manufacturer for analysis in June 2013.
During the Summer 2013, PSI worked with staff at Heath Consultants to develop a power supply module,
but this was not delivered to the ISGS with the other components, and no specifications were provided.
Additional construction of this configuration and any future field deployment would be subject to future
funding availability specifically for that purpose.  The key issue is acquisition of sufficiently robust
VSCELs that could be used to complete the construction and be field tested.

C. Remote Carbon-Dioxide Leak Detector (RCLD) Status
The RCLD was purchased by the ISGS. The device is operational, and will continue to be tested in the
laboratory and field to support ongoing IBDP activities.  Future testing will evaluate and quantify leak
detection capabilities at 5-10m standoff range.


VII.  CONCLUSIONS
This report summarizes the investigation of three prototype tunable diode laser absorption spectroscopy
(TDLAS)  sensors  for  carbon  dioxide  concentration  measurements  that  have  potential  use  in
environmental monitoring programs at CCS sites. Two of the three sensor configurations were tested and
deployed at the Illinois Basin – Decatur Project, achieving encouraging results about their suitability for
leak detection.



                                         19

The PSI Open-Path Sensor has withstood nearly 11 months of deployment at the IBDP site, monitoring
carbon dioxide levels at the active injection wellhead.  While some problems were encountered, the
majority of OPS system components proved to be effective for use as an alarm-type system intended for
personnel safety. The deployment was straightforward and required only standard installation needs (e.g.,
transceiver, reflector, and solar panel mounting). The transceiver housing, proved to be effective, keeping
the electronics and optics free of moisture, while allowing easy access of components for analysis.
Communications between the transceiver and the control computer were easily established with the radio
modems properly configured, and data-logging with the supplied software was manageable, with a typical
data rate of 91 kB/hour for 0.1 Hz sampling.  The 19.3 AH Li-Ion battery used in the OPS has been
maintained throughout deployment, and did not require replacement.

Two key problems were addressed during the OPS deployment: 1) The 30-W solar panel selected for
charging the transceiver battery was undersized for some of the weather conditions (cloud cover) faced in
the spring and fall at the installation location.  This was remedied by replacing the panel with a 65-W
option from the same manufacturer in October 2013, which to date has operated as desired even in poor
weather; 2) Thermal stresses degraded optical alignment, likely due to the laser launch assembly mounted
on the transceiver telescope. Thermal expansion of the telescope body apparently causes the laser to aim
off center of the target reflector, resulting in diminished and occasionally lost return signal.  This issue
caused some loss of data during deployment at IBDP, and has reportedly been corrected by PSI in a
methane OPS installed at natural gas leak detection test site. In addition, to make the OPS a more robust
and accurate monitoring tool, calibrating the instrument signal (and recorded data) to relatively high
accuracy measurements by other equipment should be part of standard procedures for future installations
and operation.

The construction and deployment of the in-ground sensor could not be completed due to failure of the
specialized infrared VCSEL components used in its design.  The two VSCELs acquired by PSI were
inoperable prior to delivery to the ISGS. Despite this problem, the hardware for the IGS sensor head was
delivered to the ISGS with full assembly plans and instructions. Also, preliminary deployment plans for
the sensor were discussed, including plans to acquire a power and communications tower from Heath
Consultants, using similar batteries and radio modems to the OPS device. A replacement VCSEL device
was not acquired given failure modes, lack of availability of an alternative supplier, and time constraints.
The failure of the VCSELs during laboratory testing at PSI is a major concern, and it is perhaps necessary
to consider some other options for the IGS laser component.  Despite the higher laser cost, a redesign
using the butterfly-style fiber-coupled laser may be a suitable technical option, considering the success
achieved with applying this configuration in both the OPS and the RCLD prototypes.

The RCLD performed well during this field testing program.  It was responsive to CO2 plumes in both the
laboratory setting, and in field demonstrations during the routine release of CO2 from the pipeline bleeder
valve near the well head. The device was demonstrated using surfaces of various objects as reflectors, at
distances up to 25 m. The testing showed that the RCLD responds appropriately to CO2 plumes in its
optical path (demonstrated in concentration vs. time as the transceiver beam path is passed periodically
over the plume), and that the device responds appropriately as the distance to the reflector is increased.
Because the RCLD is intended as a leak detection tool and not a quantitative measurement tool, by design
it computes concentration inaccurately when receiving weak return signals.  This effect was observed
when aiming the RCLD at diffuse backscatter targets at ranges exceeding 5m.  Similar to the OPS,


                                         20

calibration of the RCLD signal to other CO2 measurement equipment should be included as part of its
standard operating procedure.

The collaborative investigations of Physical Sciences Inc. and the Illinois State Geological Survey for this
STTR program have illustrated the uses of TDLAS-based sensors. More specifically, two types of sensor
configurations were tested successfully as CO2 monitors at the IBDP site. With refinements, similar
systems could be used at other CCS sites as part of an integrated environmental monitoring strategy.
